articleTitle: IGCT-a new emerging technology for high power, low cost inverters
abstract: Thyristor technology has, for basic physical rules, superior characteristics to transistors in blocking voltages above 2.5 kV since the plasma distributions equal those of diodes, resulting in the best trade-offs between on-state and blocking voltage. However, by adding the gate turn-off feature, GTOs have so far been constrained by a variety of unsatisfactory compromises [1], The widely used standard GTO drive technology resulted in nonhomogeneous turn-on and turn-off transients, requiring costly dv/dt- and di/dt-snubber circuits [2], [3], combined with bulky gate drive units.

articleTitle: PWM drive related bearing failures
abstract: The phenomenon of motor shaft voltages producing circulating shaft currents has been recognized since the 1920s. When a motor is operated by sinusoidal power, shaft voltages are caused by alternating flux linkages with the shaft. The linkages are associated with flux unbalance caused by: □ rotor static or dynamic eccentricity □ rotor and stator slotting □ axial cooling holes in the stator and/or rotor laminations □ shaft keyways □ rotor core support arms □ joints between segmental laminations □ directional properties of magnetic materials □ supply unbalance □ transient conditions [1].

articleTitle: EMI suppression with switching frequency modulated DC-DC converters
abstract: Usually a large amount of conducted electromagnetic interference (EMI) of a switched-mode power supply is generated by fast acting switches with sharp switching rise-and fall-times. Certain dc-dc converter topologies have peculiar input current and switching voltage wave shapes containing an infinite number of switching frequency harmonic components. However only the dc component of the input current contributes towards the average real power transfer. The remaining power contained in the harmonics is considered as conducted EMI interference and must be prevented from emanating into the supply. Furthermore, high frequency components present in the switching voltage can generate leakage current flow through converter parasitic elements thus aggravating the EMI interference. A great deal of research has been done to mitigate such conducted interference generated in de-de converters. Certain approaches in mitigating conducted EMI interference have been reported recently where the interference is suppressed at its origin. These have been carried our by selectively eliminating certain harmonics in accordance with existing EMI standards by programmed pulse width modulation or by suppressing the peak energy of a given switching frequency while redistributing the energy to additional harmonics by spread-spectrum methods. However co obtain a perfect suppression of conducted EMI, it is desirable chat these novel methods must be applied along with traditional techniques such as EMI filtering.

articleTitle: Near unity input displacement factor for current source PWM drives
abstract: In highpower/medium voltage(2300V-6900V) ac drives a PWM CSI is often used to control the speed of the motor, and the front-end rectifier is a 6 or 12 pulse thyristor rectifier (pictured on this page). Interfacing with ac mains requires low input current harmonics (to comply with recommendations such as IEEE-519), high input power factor, and good voltage/current regulation. Therefore, the thyristor rectifier must be either combined with passive/ active filters or replaced with other suitable topologies. One such topology is the PWM Current Source Rectifier (PWM CSR), Fig. 1(a). Since, in high power applications, the switching frequency is limited, the best PWM strategy is to eliminate specific harmonics while minimizing the switching frequency. Therefore, off-line Selective Harmonic Elimination can be used [1], [2], The regulation of the dc link current is achieved by either phase shifting the gating pattern or varying the modulation index [3]· Phase shifting strategy is simple but has the inherent disadvantage of obtaining a low and varying Input Displacement Factor (IDF). If modulation index control is opted for, the IDF at the rectifier terminal is unity, but as the modulation index decreases (for light loads) and because of the existence of the input filter capacitors, a low and leading power factor is obtained at the ac source. In order to achieve unity, IDF at source, i.e., including the effect of the input capacitors, closed loop control of the input line currents are proposed in the literature [4]-[6]. These schemes control and waveshape the input line currents but require on-line pattern generation and a high switching frequency, which is not feasible with GTO switches used in medium voltage applications. Feedforward techniques for compensation of the IDF are also proposed in the literature [7], [8]. These techniques are also implemented with high switching frequency [7], and some use on-line pattern generators [7], [8]. A feedforward control scheme suitable for low switching frequency circuits, which requires input voltage and current sensors to extract information about displacement angle, is proposed in [9].

articleTitle: Less-flammable liquids used in transformers
abstract: Two main types of replacement liquid have been developed, high-molecular-weight hydrocarbons and polydimethylsiloxane (silicone). These liquids are formulated to with-stand fairly large amounts of electrical arcing, and are less flammable than mineral oils. These properties qualify the liquids for use in installations where less-flammable liquids are required and where the use restrictions associated with the products are followed.

articleTitle: Using corona inception voltage for motor evaluation
abstract: Failures of the interturn insulation system of induction motors fed by pulse-width modulated (PWM) variable speed controllers have plagued the industry since the introduction of fast-switching, IGBT-based drives. The majority of these failures are attributed to high voltage stresses imposed upon the motor by the drive. Several excellent articles have been written which explain the mechanism by which substantial over-voltages can be generated at the terminals of inverter-fed motors under certain conditions (see Fig. 1) [1]-[11]. The magnitude of these voltages are a result of overshoot at the drive's output, impedance mismatch between the drive and the motor, and the PWM algorithm used by the drive[10], [11]. Problems ensue primarily (although not exclusively) in applications which have long lead lengths between the drive and the motor. In worst-case situations, voltage spikes as high as 3 times the DC bus voltage of the drive have been reported [10]-[12], This can result in a peak value of 2150V if a 460V drive system is operating at a 10% over-voltage. This voltage can be as high as 2685V in a corresponding 575V system.

articleTitle: The real cost of air conditioning load
abstract: The air-conditioning (A/C) load represents one of the major components of electric demand, especially in areas subject to extreme atmospheric conditions, such as the Gulf region. In summer, the temperature can be as high as 50°C, often combined with excessive levels of humidity. This, together with the relatively low prices of air conditioning room units and central systems (as a result of the open and highly competitive markets), and strongly subsidized energy prices, has led to an excessive impact of the air conditioning load component on the electric daily and monthly demand curves.

articleTitle: Static relays permit enhanced protection
abstract: Multi-function multi-phase static overcurrent relays, using digital technology available today, provide basic time, (51) (51GX51N) and instantaneous (50)(50G)(50N) three phase and ground overcurrent protection, and may offer some or all of the following additional functions [1][2].

articleTitle: Implementing electrical safety regulations and standards
abstract: Since the creation of OSHA in 1972, there have been continuing changes in regulations, codes and standards impacting work practices and exposure to hazardous electrical energy. These include, but are not limited to, various OSHA regulations, NFPA 70E (1988 & 1995), National Electrical Code and National Electrical Safety Code. These consensus documents are written with the intention to establish lower injury performance expectations, or to offer guidance in developing work practices that lower the risk of personnel injury. In order to have an impact in the workplace, people in the workplace must transform often general or generic expectations or guidance into changes in specific practices that may be unique for their industry, plant or work environment. A successful and effective transformation process typically requires participation and support from management, technology experts, safety professionals, and the work force (whom the changes are intended to protect). This article provides insight in the transformation process used successfully in several companies. While the details may vary from company to company, as well as from different plants within each company, the elements for success are viewed as common.

articleTitle: Device miscoordination affects plant reliability
abstract: Overcurrent protective devices are installed at strategic places in electrical systems to sense conditions that are considered to be abnormal. The sensitivity of an overcurrent device is related to the ability to sense a problem when one in fact exists. The security of the scheme is related to the ability of the device to avoid operation for a fault outside of its defined zone of protection. The selectivity of a scheme is related to the ability of the system to select the section of the power system that has a problem, and remove service from only that section. These characteristics muse be carefully considered by the protection engineer to obtain the best compromises for the given situation. This makes the design of a protection scheme an art as well as a science.

articleTitle: Dynamic system reliability study modeling
abstract: Many valuable technical methods have been developed for power distribution system reliability evaluations in recent decades [1], [2], [3]· Most power distribution system reliability studies focus on the availability of power supply at utility-customer tie points based on radial power systems. These studies evaluate load outage indices at utility-customer interface points. From the customer point of view, additional issues also deserve consideration. These can include the effect of equipment failure on power delivery quality, and the effect on system reliability due to equipment aging and maintenance quality.

articleTitle: Selection of short-circuit protection and control for Design E motors
abstract: The 1996 National Electrical Code (article 430-7 (9)) introduced the Design E motor to the Electrical Industry. A new motor designation was necessary because the Design E motor has higher efficiency, higher locked rotor current, and reduced torque requirements compared to existing NEMA motor designs. Design E motors provide increased energy savings that are important to many users. But, the possible additional costs of protective and control equipment as well as more horsepower must be part of a cost savings calculation.

articleTitle: Dust explosions in process plants
abstract: Dust explosions have caused extensive property damage and fatalities in process plants. Because of their familiarity, dusts do not get the respect that flammable vapors and gases receive. Dust explosion safety rules are entirely different from the safety rules for gases and vapors; dust is an entirely different phenomenon. Dust area classification standards and the electrical installation practices are found in the National Electrical Code. This paper will provide assistance in applying these dust standards and practices and will provide recommendations concerning their application.

articleTitle: Why train in the use of electrical heat tracing?
abstract: Increasing emphasis is being placed on training for electrical equipment in hazardous (classified) areas for many reasons. The importance of training on the proper design, installation, and maintenance of electrical equipment in hazardous (classified) locations is often discussed, planned and prioritized, but not always carried through. A lack of knowledge and understanding is the single most influential aspect of most problems. Cost has a major impact on all project and maintenance decisions, and although some may make informed wrong decisions to save money, that is not our topic.

articleTitle: Fault analysis through power quality metering
abstract: The Mead Publishing Paper Division of Mead Corporation produces a wide range of paper products in Rumford, Maine. Fig. 1 is a simplified one-line diagram for part of the mill's power system, showing the 115 kV incoming bus from the Central Maine Power Company (CMP). One 120 MVA steam turbine generator is installed in the plant for co-generation. The generator is connected to the incoming bus through a 120 MVA step-up transformer.

articleTitle: Forest product company selects IEEE Std. 841 motors
abstract: For many years now, the author has been involved in writing specifications for motors for both maintenance and major capital projects. There was not a consistent specification throughout our company for purchasing new motors. Based on past experience at existing mills, motor specifications were written for a new green field mill and included features wanted/needed that were not available on motors usually provided. After the mill was built, additional motors might be required which would match these same initial specifications. However, it became obvious that the manufacturer did not build that motor on a day to day basis. It would require a special “production run" at much higher prices than paid for the initial motors and with much longer delivery time than for standard motors. Motor maintenance repair costs for those special motors were high. Also, it was clearly time to look at company energy costs and the total cost of motor ownership.

articleTitle: History [Benjamin Garver Lamme biography]
abstract: Many of the IEEE awards carry the names of great men of the electrical and electronics engineering profession, especially those noted for their contributions in the early years of the profession. The persons are Alexander Graham Bell, Thomas Edison, B.G. Lamme, Charles Proteus Steinmetz, Nikola Tesla. Bell, Edison, and Lamme are names of some of the IEEE Major Medal awards.

articleTitle: EMI emissions of modern PWM AC drives
abstract: Electromagnetic Interference (EMI) noise is defined as an unwanted electrical signal that produces undesirable effects in a control system, such as communication errors, degraded equipment performance and malfunction or non-operation. References on the general principles of EMI are available [l]-[3], as well as methodologies on calculating radiated emissions [4]. IEEE Standard 518 applied these principles to slow switching Silicon Controlled Rectifier (SCR) dc drives in 1982 [5]. All ac Pulse Width Modulation (PWM) drives have the potential to cause EMI with adjacent sensitive equipment, when large quantities of drives are assembled in a concentrated area [6]-[11]. However, faster switching speeds of new converter/inverter topologies require an updated study of new system EMI issues created.

articleTitle: Minimizing electric bearing currents in ASD systems
abstract: During recent years, an increase in bearing failures has been seen in ASD-fed electric motors, as well as in gearboxes, and other connected machinery, caused by electric current flow through such bearings. Damage due to bearing current has sometimes been called “bearing fluting” due to the rhythmic pattern usually seen on the bearing's races [1] (see Fig. 1). Although all motor bearings may have some current flow, the existence of excessive levels of bearing current has often led to bearing failures relatively soon after start-up, within one to six months.

articleTitle: Testing update on protective clothing and equipment for electric arc exposure
abstract: Workers in electric utilities and in industry have a pressing need to be able to: 1) predict the amount of available incident energy due to electric arc exposure on their electrical transmission and distribution systems, and 2) select appropriate protective clothing and equipment to reduce injury in the event of an arc exposure. Significant progress has been made in characterizing the performance of clothing as evidenced by the development of provisional test procedures by ASTM Committee FI8 on Electrical Protective Equipment for Workers. Predicting incident energy levels based upon electrical system characteristics, however, has been a more difficult task. The inherent variability of arcs, the complex physics involved, and the wide variation in enclosures used in electrical equipment have complicated the process of estimating incident energy. A significant amount has been learned about the characteristics of electric arcs, bue additional testing is required to more accurately quantify the incident energy available at a specified distance from an electric arc on a utility or industrial electric power system.

articleTitle: Power line filter design considerations for DC-DC converters
abstract: It is well known that modern electronic systems exhibit an increased use of microelectronic circuitry for reduced size and weight, as well as for increased performance and functionality. Perhaps less well known is the fact that these systems exhibit a corresponding increased use of, and dependency upon, the dc-dc converters that supply them. The dc output voltage of these converters continues to decrease in accordance with the complexity and geometry of the microcircuits themselves. There will likely be legacy 5 V dc requirements for the foreseeable future. However, there is a definite shift toward 3.3 V dc, there is already movement toward 2.2 and 1.5 V dc and, as microelectronic geometry approaches 0.1 microns, we are likely co see de voltage requirements of less than one vole in the not coo distant future.

articleTitle: Electromagnetic compatibility issues in industrial equipment
abstract: Since 1992 all borders of the internal market of the European Union (EU) have been eliminated. Persons, goods, services and capitals move free through all EU Member States. In order to eliminate the technical barriers hampering the trades between the Member States the following actions became necessary: □ inclusion of EU directives into national laws of Member States □ harmonization of national standards with the European standards □ establishment of an European accreditation, testing and certification system, which implies a mutual recognition of validity of the test reports and conformity certificates between all Member States.

articleTitle: Better interpretation of vacuum interruptor tests
abstract: At one vacuum interrupter (VI) manufacturing facility, a single-phase, high-power circuit is used to evaluate the performance and quality of Vis, and to simulate certification tests. Precertification testing of Vis provides a great cost saving to manufacturers of vacuum circuit breakers in their development process, because it allows a them to bring new breaker models to a certification laboratory with a high degree of confidence that the breaker Vis can perform well at the targeted rating. A parallel stage in the advanced development of new VI designs involves fundamental investigations of the effects of high-current vacuum arcs on the internal components of the arcing chamber. At this level, an experimental vacuum system is used for high-speed photography of vacuum arcs between VI powder-metallurgy contacts in a demountable chamber. In this article, we step through this development process, from fundamental investigations of the arc-contact interaction to performance and precertification testing of manufactured Vis. We also describe how VI models are tested above their rated current to monitor the quality of their materials and processing.

articleTitle: Thermography, a tool for reliability and safety
abstract: It began as a routine second shift. The distribution system, although aging, has been relatively reliable. However, deep in the 480 volt switchgear, in all of the wires and connections, was a loose connection. The connection in one of the power terminations had gradually loosened and the resulting corrosion had created a high resistance termination. Heat built up over a period of time, which gradually degraded the insulation on the wire going into the connection. Suddenly, without warning, a final piece of insulation broke away exposing the bare conductor running close to the cabinet frame. An arc occurred from the wire to the frame creating a phase to ground, high resistance fault. The high resistance fault produced a current too low to be detected by the breaker or fuses. Ionized gas quickly formed, providing a low resistance path to the adjacent termination. A three phase, high energy fault soon resulted. The results can be seen in Fig. 1.

articleTitle: NEMA motor-generator standards for three-phase induction motors
abstract: The National Electrical Manufacturers Association (NEMA) Motor-Generator Standards (MG-1) have gone through numerous revisions and additions. Key information pertaining to motor performance, construction and operating conditions are provided for end users' consideration when specifying electric motors. There still is some confusion regarding how to specify electric motors and how to interpret nameplate data on existing motors. This article will provide the user with a condensed version of MG-1 to serve as a quick reference guide.

articleTitle: NEMA Design E motors and controls. What's it all about?
abstract: The NEMA Design E motor concept was developed as a result of three major driving forces. The standard for motors used in North America is MG1, Motors and Generators, of the National Electrical Manufacturer's Association (NEMA) [1]. The standards for most of the rest of the world are those of the International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC). One of the goals established by NEMA in recent years is to harmonize with IEC standards where possible. Part of the performance characteristics of the NEMA Design E motor was a result of this harmonization effort. The second area of influence is the emphasis in North America placed on energy conservation. For an electric motor this is accomplished by improvements in the motor efficiency. The third factor is ease of use. For the NEMA Design E motor to be used in existing applications it is necessary that the motor be physically interchangeable with existing motors, typically NEMA Design A or B. While the NEMA Design E motor may be a physical equivalent of a NEMA Design B motor, the differences in performance may require changes in control and protection equipment. The purpose of this paper is to present the performance differences between NEMA Design B and NEMA Design E motors and the impact chat chis may have on the control, protection and application of the motor.

articleTitle: Simplifying motor coordination studies
abstract: Low-voltage motor protection is normally the starting place for coordination studies of new industrial facilities. Also, improper low-voltage motor coordination is the source of many existing facility problems. Some engineers may frequently do coordination studies, but many engineers only occasionally do coordination studies. Trying to recall the applicable codes, standards, and references is difficult. Funds may not be available to hire “experts” for this type of study. The flow chart in Appendix A was developed to guide the “occasional” coordination engineer and to assist coordination “experts” by providing a reliable method for performing low-voltage three-phase motor coordination studies.

articleTitle: Understanding motor shaft failures
abstract: The majority of all shaft failures are caused by a combination of various stresses which act upon the rotor assembly. As long as they are kept within the intended design and application limits, shaft failures should not occur during the expected life of the motor. These stresses can be broken down into the following groups: □ Mechanical Overhung load and bending Torsional load Axial load □ Dynamic Cyclic Shock □ Residual Manufacturing processes Repair processes □ Thermal Temperature gradients Rotor bowing □ Environmental Corrosion Moisture Erosion Wear Cavitation □ Electromagnetic Side loading Out of phase reclosing

articleTitle: Electric re-regulation impact
abstract: Present-day electric utilities are the logical outgrowth of the development of electricity as a clean, reliable power source. In fact, many electric utilities started as large consumers who developed into suppliers. As dependence on electricity grew, regulation on the federal and local level increased as well. The industry essentially became a regulated monopoly in 1935. The history of the electric power system, and the growth of regulation is chronicled. As regulations grew, ancillary associations were created to solve a perceived void in some markets. These organization grew in authority, even after they were no longer necessitated by the technology of the sector. As a consequence of increased regulations, technological advancement was stymied.

articleTitle: Field motor testing: limiting risk
abstract: After several years of service, a motor is not as electrically or mechanically sound as when it was first commissioned. Motor integrity can be evaluated by conducting a series of electrical and mechanical tests.

articleTitle: The OSHA Hazard Communication Standards impact on cables
abstract: In November 1983, the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) issued a final rule for the Hazard Communication Standard (29 CFR 1910-1200). Since that time, this standard has become one of OSHA's most violated regulations. Although most of the citations issued were for failure to comply with the hazard communication program requirements, many were issued to manufacturers for not supplying Material Safety Data Sheets (MSDSs) and hazard warning labels for the products they produce. Manufactured goods which are considered an "Article" are exempt from having MSDSs and labels; thus a manufacturer's interpretation of “Article” can be the deciding factor in determining whether or not a MSDS is required for a finished product. Many of the citations issued to manufacturers who failed to develop and provide MSDSs and labels for their products were at least partially due to misinterpretation of the confusing definition of "Article” in the standard.

articleTitle: Guest Editorial
abstract: The IAS Magazine made its debut with the January/February 1995 issue. With few exceptions, the articles which appear in the magazine are based on papers presented at various IAS-sponsored conferences and recommended by an IAS technical committee. As Chair of the IAS Education Department, I am a member of the Editorial Board for the Magazine. At its meeting at the 1997 IAS Annual Meeting in New Orleans, the Editorial Board discussed different methods for soliciting articles for the magazine. One idea that emerged from that meeting was a special issue on a topic of interest to IAS members. Electromagnetic interference and compatibility (EMI/EMC) was selected to be the focus of this special issue, which I agreed to coordinate. Historically, EMI/EMC has been studied in the context of communication systems. However, with advances in electrical technology, engineers who design and use modern electrical power equipment must be aware of EMI/EMC.

articleTitle: Errata [Better interpritation of vacumm interrupter tests]
Letters
abstract: Dear Sir: Many years ago, a former head of the American Standards Association called standards a necessary evil. Standards are used because they have the potential to save effort, especially thinking effort (great thinkers are always in very scarce supply, very good thinkers are very rare, and good thinkers aren't so rare) and because using standards is economical and may be required by law.

articleTitle: Process seals: danger and solution [Letters]
abstract: A process seal leak is disastrous if hydrocarbons enter electrical systems. But hydro-carbons processes must use electrical systems to control and monitor. This requires complex seals to separate the hydrocarbons, inside the processes, from the electrical systems outside. National Electrical Code, Article 501-5, (f), describes how seal systems to separate hydrocarbons from electrical systems must be made, including means of detecting failure: “connect seal to ‘T’ drain via conduit (makes leak visible), follow with another conduit terminated in a poured conduit seal (prevent leak entering arcing electrical device).”

articleTitle: Awards
abstract: The Awards Department of the IEEE, IAS Proudly Announces the 1998 Award Recipients. The IEEE named one IAS member as a recipient of a Medal: C. James Erickson for the IEEE Medal for Engineering Excellence. The Society Executive Board named the 1998 recipients of the major Society Awards to be: □ Donald W. Novotny for the IAS Outstanding Achievement Award □ F. A. (Tony) Furfari for the IAS Distinguished Service Award □ Iqbal Husain for the IAS Outstanding Young Member Award

articleTitle: Charles A. Ruch 1915-1998 Westinghouse Electric Communicator, Historian, Curator
abstract: The International Appliance Technical Conference (IATC) and IEEE IAS Appliance Industry Committee (AIC) are jointly celebrating their 50th anniversary this year. Although the AIC is an active and fully functioning committee of the IAS, many members are unfamiliar with the AIC and even less familiar with the IATC. This month's article explores some of che history of both organizations.

articleTitle: History - Charles Concordia - 1999 IEEE Medal of Honor
abstract: Dr. Charles Concordia is the recipient of the 1999 IEEE Medal of Honor, one of the Institute's most prestigious awards. Concordia's name is closely associated with the Power Engineering Society (PES) of the IEEE, more so than the other constituent societies. Although he may be more widely recognized by members of the PES, certainly his work has greatly influenced and benefited the IAS. In coming months you will hear more about this award and about Dr. Concordia. The June issue of Spectrum usually features an article on the current year's recipient of the Medal of Honor. In anticipation of the forthcoming celebrations, IAS Magazine profiled this fascinating personality and renowned engineer.
